title: Youngwon Kim
text:
I build clinical AI systems — and the evidence that they work.
      Machine Learning Postdoctoral Researcher · Truveta · Bellevue, WA
    
    
      
    
  

  
    I am a machine learning researcher trained in measurement science. On
    Truveta's Intelligence ML team I work across the model lifecycle on longitudinal
    electronic health records. I train clinical foundation models,
    including reinforcement learning that steers generated patient journeys toward
    real ones. I build the benchmarks and
    evaluations that test them, and the pipelines (MCP
    tools, agent systems, dashboards) that carry them into clinical workflows.
    Measurement science is the unusual part of my background. A Ph.D. in
    measurement and statistics (University of Washington) and
    postdoctoral training in Harvard's CARES Lab (Causality,
    Applications, and Research in Education and Statistics) gave me tools that
    machine learning rarely borrows: validity theory, latent variable models,
    reliability analysis, and the design of randomized trials. I have applied them
    to very different data, from student essays and psychological surveys to
    electronic health records.
    Across all of it, I ask whether a number means what we think it means,
    whether it is a benchmark score, an LLM grader, or a model-estimated
    patient-reported outcome. I ask it at every stage, not just at the end. Validity
    is not a final step; it is a design constraint.

title: Research
text:
My work follows a model through its life — trained, evaluated, deployed — with
  one discipline underneath all of it: measurement. Each stage asks its own version
  of the same question: does this number mean what we think it means?
  Most of the code behind this work is proprietary to Truveta. The papers,
  abstracts, and write-ups linked below are its public record.



  01 · Train
  Foundation models trained on patient journeys can predict what happens next — if the modeling respects the data
  Does a generated patient journey contain the diagnoses and biomarkers that real ones do?
  
    On Truveta's Intelligence ML team I train oncology-specific and
    general-purpose clinical foundation models on longitudinal electronic health
    records. Because the training data are messy, the events that matter most —
    specific diagnoses, key biomarkers — are the ones a plain generative model gets
    wrong. So I am adding reinforcement learning that pulls generated
    patient journeys toward real ones.
    Clean inputs are part of training, not a preliminary: the same models impute
    missing units of measure and derive health-state transitions from the data rather
    than by assumption. I also build ML and LLM risk models for cancer and heart
    failure.
  
  
    Related: ISPOR 2026·Colorectal cancer LLM (AMIA)·Write-ups
  



  02 · Evaluate
  An evaluation is a measurement instrument, and should be validated like one
  Does the score mean what we think it means?
  
    Benchmarks and model-as-judge systems are instruments that rarely report their
    psychometric properties. I build evaluations that establish validity and
    reliability before a metric is used to make a claim. For our patient-journey
    foundation model, that means a multi-level evaluation framework,
    from checks of the model itself to the quality of what it generates.
    Its benchmarks widen in stages, from one cancer to all cancers to diseases
    across the general population. Simulations test whether generated journeys follow
    clinically plausible progression.
    In heart failure, EHR-based estimation of KCCQ scores turns on
    whether a model-derived score means what the patient-reported instrument means.
    Earlier, at Harvard, I tested LLM graders against human scores for high-stakes
    essay scoring, the reliability question behind any model-graded evaluation, and
    helped develop rcttext, an R package for analyzing text outcomes
    in randomized trials.
  
  
    Related: KCCQ (medRxiv)·LLMs vs. ML for essay scoring·AEFP & JSM 2024
  



  03 · Deploy
  Tooling decides whether a good model ever reaches anyone
  Will the people who need the signal see it in time, and in context?
  
    A model that only runs in a notebook has not been deployed. I build the layer
    that carries one into use: MCP tools for clinical NLU that pull
    structured disease status and patient trajectories out of messy real-world text,
    and agent frameworks — multi-agent and deep-agent
    architectures, LangChain pipelines — that interpret what the models return.
    Around them sit automated prompt optimization, interactive dashboards, and
    end-to-end pipeline monitoring, so the people making decisions can interrogate a
    prediction rather than just receive it. Most of the distance between a promising
    result and a used one is infrastructure.
  
  
    Related: CV·Write-ups
  



  04 · Foundations
  Classical measurement theory and modern machine learning improve each other
  What are we actually measuring?
  
    My doctoral work was on factor analysis and prediction algorithms, and I
    keep returning to the seam between them: gradient boosting to improve
    factor-retention decisions under measurement error, penalized estimation
    (Lasso, adaptive Lasso, and the minimax concave penalty) for exploratory
    measurement modeling, and network analysis for quantifying item process
    data.
    Latent variable models were built to handle noisy, partial, indirect
    observation of something you cannot measure directly. That is also a fair
    description of an electronic health record.
  
  
    Related: AERA 2024·IMPS 2023·NCME 2021
